I · The approval path

01

Dashboard

Where the shift starts

Four counters, then the queue. Eight schedules configured, sixteen packs published today, eight waiting on a reviewer, twenty anomalies open. Every figure in Key Figures on the right carries the count of source records it was computed from, and each chip under it opens that record.

02

Approvals

Nothing is approved sight-unseen

Seven of the eight reports in this queue are stamped Not opened. That column is not decoration — the API refuses an approval on any report whose reviewer has not opened it, so the badge and the rule are the same fact.

03

Quarterly Business Review

Figures, then commentary — in that order

Q2 2026 against the same quarter last year. Revenue down 28.2%, margin down 18.2%, win rate down 33.3% — surfaced as Needs attention above the tables. The prose underneath is generated from these already-computed numbers and cannot alter one of them; that separation is what the line under the header states plainly.

04

Drill-through

Open the number, see the row

Clicking any source chip pulls the record straight from the connected system — here invoice INV-2026-1134, SAR 616,187.81, Dammam Logistics Co., paid. This is what “100% of figures traceable to a source record” means when it is a property of the code rather than a promise in a document.

05

Approve, then publish

The gate holds in both directions

Once the report has been opened, approval is accepted and the run moves to Published with delivery recorded against its recipients. Publishing is the only path that sets a publication timestamp, and it will not run on anything that is not already approved.

II · Chat with data

06

Chat with data

An answer, not a sentence

“Total sales this month vs last month.” The agent resolves the metric and the period, then returns the narrative, KPI cards, a trend, a summary table, the four invoices behind it, and the query it ran. It also flags that August is still in progress and is being compared against a complete month.

07

Follow-up

Context carries across turns

“Now split that by business unit” — no metric named, no period restated. The conversation remembers both and returns the breakdown with each unit's share. Distribution leads at 49% of the month.

08

When it doesn't know

Refusing to guess is a feature

“What is the vibe of the company” resolves to nothing in the metric registry, so the agent says so, marks its confidence low, and offers the measures it does have. A plausible-sounding invented answer is the one outcome finance cannot audit.

09

Same question, different role

Scope is enforced, not hidden

Switched to Mansour Tayeb, a viewer on the Sales team, asking the same receivables question. The refusal names the module and the role rather than quietly returning nothing. Note the sidebar counts drop to what this person may actually see: two approvals, ten anomalies.

III · Detection and the trail

10

Anomalies

Ranked, costed, and routed

Twenty open findings across business data and software usage — an edit to a closed accounting period worth SAR 184,500, a bulk deletion of 112 CRM records, a sign-in from an unexpected country. Severity, module and financial exposure are on every row; the ones marked Alerted did not wait for the next report.

11

One finding, in full

What, why, how much, who, and what next

Every item answers the same five questions and links the records it was raised from. A rule that cannot supply all of them does not fire. False positive both suppresses the finding and tightens the rule that raised it, which is how the false-positive rate is driven down rather than tolerated.

12

Audit log

Who saw what, when, and what changed

Generation, viewing, approval, rejection, publication, anomaly triage, rule changes and every chat answer land here, with the actor and the payload. The approval I made two steps ago is in this list, stamped with the moment I opened the report first.

13

Detection rules

Configuration, not a code release

Twelve rules with editable thresholds, detection and false-positive counts per rule, and the sensitivity multiplier that false-positive marks apply. The other tabs hold the reporting calendar and the metric registry every figure resolves through.

IV · The same rules, at the API

—

The screens are not the enforcement

Every guard answers the same way without a browser

A user interface that disables a button is a suggestion. These are the same rules called directly against the running API — approval refused until the report has been opened, a rejection refused without a real reason, publication refused on anything unapproved, and a viewer refused outright.

live against localhost:8000
$ target: Executive Dashboard Report (run 21), never opened

POST /approvals/runs/21/approve            -> 409  Open the report before approving it — approvals are recorded against a review.
GET  /reports/runs/21                       -> 200  (opening is what records the review)
POST /approvals/runs/21/reject  'wrong'      -> 422  String should have at least 10 characters
POST /approvals/runs/21/approve  (reopened)  -> 200  status=approved
POST /approvals/runs/21/publish              -> 200  status=published delivery=delivered
POST /approvals/runs/21/publish  (again)     -> 409  Only an approved report can be published to recipients.
POST /approvals/runs/18/approve  as viewer -> 403  Your role (viewer) is not permitted to approve.

Captured at 1440×920 in Chromium against commit 5a2f6741. The seed is deterministic, so these counts reproduce on a fresh database. To run it yourself: uvicorn main:app --port 8000 in backend/, then npm run dev in frontend/.
